newsitem.title: FRANCE: French doctors stay out, Paris hints at softening.
newsitem.headline: French doctors stay out, Paris hints at softening.

text.p: French junior hospital doctors, in the fourth week of a strike against state plans to cap health spending, kept up the pressure on Thursday amid hints of new flexibility from the government.
Demonstrators, numbering about 3,000 according to police, marched through Paris to denounce the government plan, which they say will lead to rationing of public health care.

"Good health or the Juppe plan, you choose," screamed a banner at the head of the march, referring to conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe's plan to fine doctors if their region overshoots pre-set spending limits.

The strike, which has spread to 23 of 26 French teaching hospitals, has developed into a test of Juppe's resolve to cut public deficits to allow France to qualify for the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
The government has rejected the junior doctors' demands and accused them of promoting their own sectional interests at the expense of patients.
Thursday's turnout was much smaller than a demonstration on March 27 in which at least 10,000 junior hospital doctors from all over France marched in Paris against the reforms.
Hours earlier, a marathon session of talks between the strikers and Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot yielded some of the first conciliatory statements in the 23-day-old conflict.
While vowing to stick to their demands, the strikers promised to stop blocking railways and roads.
"Firmness and mobilisation are still on our agenda...This is no time for doctors to go back to work as their demands have not yet been met," a spokesman for the strikers said.
After the talks, Barrot hinted he might be prepared to negotiate on the issue of fining doctors for overspending, a key concession the doctors have been demanding.
"As for the fine or solidarity payment, there is still room to improve the way these possible fines would be paid," he said.
Unions representing the junior doctors are due to meet Barrot and junior Health Minister Herve Gaymard again on Friday.
Thursday's march brought together the striking junior doctors, other hospital staff unhappy about cuts in medical funding and the Communist-led CGT, one of France's biggest labour unions.

Unions representing specialists in private practice, who have opposed the reforms from the time they were announced in late 1995 and who have allied themselves with the junior doctors, also joined Thursday's protest.
They have called for a national demonstration on April 13.
